clue.text: He was schooled in mystery, he said

definitions.text: He was schooled in mystery, he said

parts.words: He was schooled in mystery, he said
parts.note: in Lewis Carroll's Alice, a melancholy creature claims his school lessons included 'Mystery, ancient and modern', a pun on history

explanation.surface: Someone boasts of an education in the arcane arts.
explanation.walkthrough: The character in Alice's Adventures in Wonderland lists his lessons as Reeling, Writhing and 'Mystery, ancient and modern', so 'mystery' here is his garbling of history, not the occult.
explanation.definitionFit: The Carroll character who tells Alice of his sea-school curriculum is the sad creature named after a soup made to imitate one.

clue.text: Some doctors' prescriptions include wine

definitions.text: wine

indicators.note: include says the letters sit inside the words before it

explanation.surface: Physicians sometimes recommend a glass of claret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'include' signals letters running across 'Some doctors'': soME DOCtors.
explanation.definitionFit: A red Bordeaux from the left bank of the Gironde is a classic claret.

clue.text: But it's not 33⅓ yards long

definitions.text: But it's not 33⅓ yards long

parts.note: thirty-three and a third yards is a hundred feet, and the creature named for having a hundred feet is not that long

explanation.surface: Something falls short of a stated length.
explanation.walkthrough: 33⅓ yards is 100 feet; the many-legged creature's name means 'hundred feet', though it is nowhere near that length.
explanation.definitionFit: The many-legged arthropod takes its name from the Latin for a hundred feet.

clue.text: What the Walrus said, to be up to date

definitions.text: What the Walrus said
to be up to date

explanation.surface: A character from a poem gives a modern opinion.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis Carroll's poem 'The Walrus and the Carpenter' contains the line beginning 'The time has come, the Walrus said'.
explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's Walrus opens his talk of shoes and ships with these words; and when a moment arrives its appointed date is up.

clue.text: Operation calculated to produce tears

definitions.text: Operation calculated to produce tears

parts.note: 'tears' are rips rather than weeping, so the operation is one of tearing apart

explanation.surface: A procedure is designed to make someone cry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'tears' looks like crying; it is rips, rhyming with 'bears'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ripping something apart violently is an action that leaves rips.

clue.text: Behold the poet doing his work bit by bit

definitions.text: doing his work bit by bit

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning behold
a rimer is a writer of rhymes, so a poet

explanation.surface: We are shown a poet composing gradually.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit by bit' looks like gradually; a lorimer makes bits, spurs and other metal fittings for horses' harness.
explanation.definitionFit: A maker of horses' bridle bits and harness metalwork produces his goods one bit after another.

clue.text: No sound reason for this admonition

definitions.text: No sound reason for this admonition

parts.words: No sound reason for this admonition
parts.note: read 'No sound' as the purpose of the warning: the reprimand is given so that there will be silence

explanation.surface: A scolding seems to have been handed out without good grounds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No sound reason' looks like 'no valid reason', but 'sound' means noise: the admonition exists to get no sound.
explanation.definitionFit: A word said to silence someone is an admonition whose whole purpose is quiet.

clue.text: Trust the Association to get Jack, on the staff!

definitions.text: Trust the Association to get Jack, on the staff!

parts.words: Trust the Association to get Jack, on the staff
parts.note: trust and association both mean a joining together, and that word with Jack is the British flag flown on a flagstaff

explanation.surface: A trade body predictably hires someone called Jack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a new employee and 'staff' like personnel; the Union Jack is the British flag, run up a flagstaff.
explanation.definitionFit: A trade association or combination is a joining together, and that word precedes Jack in the British flag's name.

clue.text: But it needn't characterize proceedings on fast-days

definitions.text: But it needn't characterize proceedings on fast-days

parts.words: But it needn't characterize proceedings on fast-days
parts.note: 'fast' is read as quick rather than going without food, and a holy day is a high day, so quick proceedings on high days

explanation.surface: Religious days of abstinence need not be conducted in any particular manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast-days' looks like days of fasting, but the answer reads as a rapid pace on high days.
explanation.definitionFit: Very rapid motion is what 'fast' suggests, quite apart from days of abstinence.

clue.text: Not the walk-over one would expect at bridge

definitions.text: Not the walk-over one would expect at bridge

parts.words: Not the walk-over one would expect at bridge
parts.note: 'bridge' is not the card game but a way across water; a row of rocks gives a way over a stream instead of a bridge

explanation.surface: A card game turns out not to be an easy win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'walk-over' and 'bridge' suggest an easy victory at cards; the walk over a stream here is on a row of rocks instead of a bridge.
explanation.definitionFit: A line of flat rocks placed across a stream lets people walk over without a bridge.

clue.text: Medieval dark-room, but not for photographers

definitions.text: Medieval dark-room, but not for photographers

parts.words: Medieval dark-room, but not for photographers
parts.note: a dark room in a medieval castle was the windowless cell below ground where prisoners were kept

explanation.surface: A gloomy historic chamber is not a place for developing film.
explanation.definitionFit: The windowless prison cell beneath a castle keep was a dark chamber of the Middle Ages.

clue.text: The Dean in a bad way in Sussex

definitions.text: The Dean in a bad way in Sussex

parts.words: The Dean in a bad way in Sussex
parts.note: a coastal village near Brighton in East Sussex has a name that reads as a dean who is decaying, so the clue wants the decaying part

explanation.surface: A churchman in a southern English county is in poor health.
explanation.walkthrough: Rottingdean is a village on the Sussex coast near Brighton; split after its seventh letter it describes a dean in a bad way, and the answer is the word for that bad way.
explanation.definitionFit: Being in a bad way, decaying or going off, is what the word before 'dean' in the village name describes.

clue.text: Subject of a papal essay ?

definitions.text: Subject of a papal essay ?

parts.note: 'papal' refers not to a pontiff but to the poet Alexander Pope, whose verse essay of 1711 discussed literary judgement

explanation.surface: A pontiff's written treatise takes up some theme.
explanation.walkthrough: Alexander Pope wrote 'An Essay on Criticism'; 'papal' is turned from 'of the Pope' to 'of Pope'.
explanation.definitionFit: The faultfinding appraisal of literature was the theme of Alexander Pope's famous essay in verse.

clue.text: Poles are at hand to get them going

definitions.text: Poles are at hand to get them going

parts.words: Poles are at hand to get them going
parts.note: the poles are long wooden staves pushed against a riverbed, not people from Poland, and they propel flat boats

explanation.surface: People from Poland are ready to help start something.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Poles' with its capital looks like people from Poland; it is the long staves used to push flat-bottomed boats along rivers such as the Cam.
explanation.definitionFit: Flat-bottomed river boats are propelled by a person pushing a long staff against the bottom.

clue.text: Island to con for building material

definitions.text: Island

indicators.note: 'X to con for building material' says X added to the word con gives the material, so the material less con leaves X

parts.note: concrete is a building material
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone plans to swindle an islander out of supplies for construction.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to con for' means that putting CON before the answer gives a building material, CONCRETE; removing CON leaves the island.
explanation.definitionFit: The largest Greek island, south of the Aegean mainland, is home to the Minoan palace of Knossos.

clue.text: Chambers to be kept bone-dry?

definitions.text: Chambers to be kept bone-dry?

parts.note: 'bone-dry' is read as dry places for keeping bones, the underground burial vaults of ancient Rome

explanation.surface: Some rooms must be kept free of damp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bone-dry' means very dry, but here the chambers are kept dry for the bones of the dead stored in them.
explanation.definitionFit: Underground burial galleries, like those under Rome, are chambers where human bones are kept.

clue.text: Anti-bugging device ?

definitions.text: Anti-bugging device ?

parts.note: the bugs are not hidden microphones but microbes, and the device is something that kills them

explanation.surface: A gadget defeats hidden listening equipment.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bugging' suggests espionage, but a bug is also an informal word for a microbe.
explanation.definitionFit: A disinfectant that destroys microbes works against the informal 'bugs' of illness.

clue.text: "And the same to you!"

definitions.text: And the same to you!

parts.note: a retort wishing back exactly what was said, the same in every respect

explanation.surface: Someone returns an insult or a greeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Being exactly alike in every detail is what 'the same' means.

clue.text: They cannot remain so for over seven years

definitions.text: They cannot remain so for over seven years

parts.words: They cannot remain so for over seven years
parts.note: the ages from thirteen to nineteen span exactly seven years, so nobody stays in that group longer

explanation.surface: Some condition is said to be limited to a set term of years.
explanation.definitionFit: Young people aged thirteen to nineteen pass through that span of ages in seven years.

clue.text: Help set the make-up for a girl

definitions.text: a girl

indicators.note: make-up is the way something is put together, so the letters are composed afresh

explanation.surface: Someone helps apply cosmetics for a young woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'make-up' looks like cosmetics; it is the anagram signal on HELP SET.
explanation.definitionFit: Elspeth is a Scottish female first name, a form of Elizabeth.

clue.text: Whoever makes this for a painter has his work cut out

definitions.text: Whoever makes this for a painter has his work cut out

parts.words: Whoever makes this for a painter has his work cut out
parts.note: 'has his work cut out' is read literally: the maker must cut the pattern out of a sheet for the painter to dab through

explanation.surface: Producing something for an artist is a demanding job.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has his work cut out' usually means faces a hard task; here the work literally is cut out of a sheet.
explanation.definitionFit: A cut-out sheet through which paint is dabbed to reproduce a pattern is a painter's template.

clue.text: .Vice of those found wanting, perhaps

definitions.text: Vice of those found wanting, perhaps

parts.words: Vice of those found wanting, perhaps
parts.note: 'wanting' is read as desiring more rather than falling short, and the vice is that of always wanting

explanation.surface: Those who fail a test may have a moral failing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Found wanting' usually means found inadequate; here it means found desiring, and the vice is avarice.
explanation.definitionFit: Avarice, one of the seven deadly sins, is the failing of people always wanting more.

clue.text: Like the centre of a town

definitions.text: Like the centre of a town

parts.words: Like the centre of a town
parts.note: a town's central municipal buildings are commonly called by a phrase whose first word means relating to a town

explanation.surface: Something resembles the heart of an urban area.
explanation.walkthrough: A town's municipal heart is its 'civic centre'; the answer is also a palindrome, the same letters either side of its middle V.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective for things relating to a town or its citizens describes a municipal centre.

clue.text: Milton's poetical siren

definitions.text: Milton's poetical siren

parts.note: in Milton's 'At a Solemn Music' voice and poetry are called a 'blest pair of Sirens'; one of the pair is poetry itself

explanation.surface: A seductive figure appears in Milton's poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: Milton's ode 'At a Solemn Music' opens 'Blest pair of Sirens, pledges of heaven's joy, / Sphere-born harmonious sisters, Voice and Verse'.
explanation.definitionFit: Milton calls Voice and poetry's metrical lines the two harmonious Sirens in 'At a Solemn Music'.

clue.text: Watchman might cope with tarts, possibly

definitions.text: Watchman

indicators.note: possibly says the letters of the words may be arranged some other way

explanation.surface: A guard might manage with some pastries.
explanation.walkthrough: 'possibly' signals an anagram of COPE and TARTS together.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who watches an event is an onlooker, a person keeping watch.

clue.text: This race is often a touch-and-go affair

definitions.text: This race is often a touch-and-go affair

parts.words: This race is often a touch-and-go affair
parts.note: 'touch-and-go' is read literally: one runner touches the next, who then goes, as in a team race with handovers

explanation.surface: A contest is frequently a close-run thing.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touch-and-go' means uncertain; here a runner must touch or hand over to a teammate before the teammate can go.
explanation.definitionFit: A team race in which each runner hands over to the next is run in stages.

clue.text: As a French writer he appeared to prosper

definitions.text: As a French writer he appeared to prosper

parts.words: As a French writer he appeared to prosper
parts.note: 'prosper' is the first name of the nineteenth-century French author of Carmen, so as a writer he appeared under it

explanation.surface: A Frenchman seemed to do well from his writing.
explanation.walkthrough: The author of the novella Carmen was Prosper Mérimée; 'appeared to prosper' means published under the name Prosper.
explanation.definitionFit: The French author of Carmen and Colomba wrote under his given name, Prosper.

clue.text: Coming to the point, figuratively speaking

definitions.text: Coming to the point, figuratively speaking

parts.words: Coming to the point, figuratively speaking
parts.note: 'figuratively' means in terms of geometric figures, and a figure that tapers to a single point is described

explanation.surface: A speaker finally gets to the heart of the matter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Coming to the point' sounds like getting to the gist, and 'figuratively' like metaphorically; both refer to a solid shape tapering to an apex.
explanation.definitionFit: A cone-shaped solid narrows from its round base to a single apex.

clue.text: Appear to observe many

definitions.text: Appear

parts.note: to observe is to see
M is the Roman numeral for a thousand, so many

explanation.surface: Someone is asked to turn up to watch a crowd.
explanation.definitionFit: To appear is to give an impression of being something.

clue.text: "A Doll's House", for example? Easy!

definitions.text: "A Doll's House", for example
Easy

explanation.surface: Ibsen's drama is held up as an example of something simple.
explanation.walkthrough: A Doll's House is Ibsen's play, but here it is a game of house with dolls, the sort of play a child enjoys.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing house with dolls is a game a youngster plays; and something very easy is said to be no harder than such a game.
